title: Improving Teaching Practice At The Individual Level
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino considers how an individual teacher can keep improving, using Dylan Wiliam's line that every teacher needs to improve because they can be even better. Her simple mantra is to identify a problem and then find an evidence-based solution. She recounts adopting Takeaway Homework from Twitter without checking it against how students learn, which added work and had no effect on learning. She now identifies problems by reading about learning, observing other teachers and reflecting on what students think and do, and finds solutions the same way, one aspect of teaching at a time. She notes that this needs time and ends with a plea to school leaders to cut admin, data and behaviour follow-up. It is Practice & Culture as it concerns teacher professional growth.
points: Magpieing ideas from social media without checking the need or how to evaluate them wastes effort.
Better knowledge of how students learn lets a teacher see problems, such as weak questioning, they could not see before.
Takeaway Homework solved motivation but ignored the research on learning and so created work without impact.
Improvement should focus on one aspect of teaching at a time, perfected through practice before moving on.
School leaders should protect teacher time for reflection by reducing admin, data and behaviour follow-up.
quotes: The problem was I didn’t consider context or if I even needed to implement these things. Magpieing ideas without thought of the need for them, their implementation or consideration of how to evaluate them is not helpful.

There may have been good advice buried underneath these generic comments but as some of these came from non-specialists, there were no concrete solutions to my problems. So I had to look elsewhere for my solutions.
This knowledge helps me identify problems I never even thought of before. For instance, I never really thought about my questioning. Before I would have asked a few questions that were mostly recall.

This is why it didn’t have the desired impact in the long-term. Takeaway Homework became another thing I implemented that created unnecessary work for me (tracking what dishes students were choosing each time so they didn’t just always pick ‘Write a Tweet about…’) and that had no effect on student learning.
Self-improvement takes time. I have been lucky that I have the freedom, autonomy and time to read, observe and reflect on my teaching practice.

So a plea to school leaders: give your staff the time to reflect on their teaching practice. Actively reduce the time spent on admin, data and behaviour so teachers can focus on doing their best for their students.
